content.heading: 5.9 Applications to Markov Chains
content.paragraph: The Markov chains described in this section are used as mathematical models of a wide variety of situations in biology, business, chemistry, engineering, physics, and elsewhere. In each case, the model is used to describe an experiment or measurement that is performed many times in the same way, where the outcome of each trial of the experiment will be one of several specified possible outcomes, and where the outcome of one trial depends only on the immediately preceding trial.
For example, if the population of a city and its suburbs were measured each year, then a vector such as

could indicate that $60\%$ of the population lives in the city and $40\%$ in the suburbs. The decimals in $\textbf{x}_{0}$ add up to $1$ because they account for the entire population of the region. Percentages are more convenient for our purposes here than population totals.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A vector with nonnegative entries that add up to $1$ is called a probability vector. A stochastic matrix is a square matrix whose columns are probability vectors.

content.paragraph: A Markov chain is a sequence of probability vectors $\textbf{x}_{0},\textbf{x}_{1},\textbf{x}_{2},\ldots$, together with a stochastic matrix $P$, such that
Thus the Markov chain is described by the first-order difference equation

When a Markov chain of vectors in $\textbf{ℝ}^{n}$ describes a system or a sequence of experiments, the entries in $\textbf{x}_{k}$ list, respectively, the probabilities that the system is in each of $n$ possible states, or the probabilities that the outcome of the experiment is one of $n$ possible outcomes. For this reason, $\textbf{x}_{k}$ is often called a state vector.

example.paragraph: Section 1.10 examined a model for population movement between a city and its suburbs. See Figure 1. The annual migration between these two parts of the metropolitan region was governed by the migration matrix $M$:

Then the initial distribution of the population in the region is given previously by $\textbf{x}_{0}$ in (1). What is the distribution of the population in 2021? In 2022?

content.heading: Predicting the Distant Future
content.paragraph: The most interesting aspect of Markov chains is the study of a chain’s long-term behavior. For instance, what can be said in Example 2 about the voting after many elections have passed (assuming that the given stochastic matrix continues to describe the transition percentages from one election to the next)? Or, what happens to the population distribution in Example 1 “in the long run”? Here our work on eigenvalues and eigenvectors becomes helpful.

note.title: Theorem ﻿10﻿
note.heading: Theorem ﻿10﻿
Stochastic Matrices
note.paragraph: If $P$ is a stochastic matrix, then $1$ is an eigenvalue of $P$.

content.heading: Proof﻿
content.paragraph: Since the columns of $P$ sum to $1$, the rows of $P^{T}$ will also sum to $1$. Let $\textbf{e}$ represent the vector for which every entry is $1$. Notice that multiplying $P^{T}$ by $\textbf{e}$ has the effect of adding up the values in each row, hence $P^{T}\textbf{e} = \textbf{e}$, establishing that $\textbf{e}$ is an eigenvector of $P^{T}$ with eigenvalue $1$. Since $P$ and $P^{T}$ have the same eigenvalues (Exercise 20 in Section 5.2), $1$ is also an eigenvalue of $P$.

In the next example, we see that the vectors generated in a Markov chain are almost the same as the vectors generated using the power method outlined in Section 5.8—the only difference is that in a Markov chain, the vectors are not scaled at each step. Based on our experience from Section 5.8, as $k$ increases we expect $\textbf{x}_{k}\rightarrow\textbf{q}$, where $\textbf{q}$ is an eigenvector of $P$.

content.heading: Steady-State Vectors
content.paragraph: If $P$ is a stochastic matrix, then a steady-state vector (orequilibrium vector) for $P$ is a probability vector $\textbf{q}$ such that

In Theorem 10, it is established that $1$ is an eigenvalue of any stochastic matrix. It can be shown that $1$ is actually the largest eigenvalue of a stochastic matrix and the associated eigenvector can be chosen to be a steady-state vector. In Example 3, q is a steady-state vector for $P$.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: The probability vector $\textbf{q} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{r} .375 \\ .625 \end{array} \right\rbrack$ is a steady-state vector for the population migration matrix $M$ in Example 1, because

content.paragraph: If the total population of the metropolitan region in Example 1 is $1$ million, then $\textbf{q}$ from Example 4 would correspond to having $375,000$ persons in the city and $625,000$ in the suburbs. At the end of one year, the migration out of the city would be $(.05)(375,000) = 18,750$ persons, and the migration into the city from the suburbs would be $(.03)(625,000) = 18,750$ persons. As a result, the population in the city would remain the same. Similarly, the suburban population would be stable.
The next example shows how to find a steady-state vector. Notice that we are just finding an eigenvector associated with the eigenvalue $1$ and then scaling it to create a probability vector.

content.paragraph: The next theorem shows that what happened in Example 3 is typical of many stochastic matrices. We say that a stochastic matrix is regular if some matrix power $P^{k}$ contains only strictly positive entries. For $P$ in Example 3,
Since every entry in $P^{2}$ is strictly positive, $P$ is a regular stochastic matrix.

Also, we say that a sequence of vectors, $\textbf{x}_{k}$ for $k = 1,2,\ldots,$ converges to a vector $\textbf{q}$ as $k\rightarrow\text{∞}$, if the entries in $\textbf{x}_{k}$ can be made as close as desired to the corresponding entries in $\textbf{q}$ by taking $k$ sufficiently large.

note.title: ﻿﻿﻿Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.heading: ﻿﻿﻿Theorem ﻿11﻿
note.paragraph: If $P$ is an $n \times n$ regular stochastic matrix, then $P$ has a unique steady-state vector $\textbf{q}$. Further, if $\textbf{x}_{0}$ is any initial state and $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = P\textbf{x}_{k}$ for $k = 0,1,2,\ldots,$ then the Markov chain $\{\textbf{x}_{k}\}$ converges to $\textbf{q}$ as $k\rightarrow\text{∞}$.

content.paragraph: This theorem is proved in standard texts on Markov chains. The amazing part of the theorem is that the initial state has no effect on the long-term behavior of the Markov chain.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: In Example 2, what percentage of the voters are likely to vote for the Republican candidate in some election many years from now, assuming that the election outcomes form a Markov chain?
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: If you want to compute the precise entries of the steady-state vector by hand, it is better to recognize that it is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $1$ rather than to pick some initial vector $\textbf{x}_{0}$ and compute $\textbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{x}_{k}$ for some large value of $k$. You have no way of knowing how many vectors to compute, and you cannot be sure of the limiting values of the entries in $\textbf{x}_{k}$.

A better approach is to compute the steady-state vector and then appeal to Theorem 11. Given $P$ as in Example 2, form $P - I$ by subtracting $1$ from each diagonal entry in $P$. Then row reduce the augmented matrix:
Recall from earlier work with decimals that the arithmetic is simplified by multiplying each row by $10$.1

The general solution of $(P - I)\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ is $x_{1} = \frac{9}{4}x_{3},x_{2} = \frac{15}{4}x_{3}$, and $x_{3}$ is free. Choosing $x_{3} = 4$, we obtain a basis for the solution space whose entries are integers, and from this we easily find the steady-state vector whose entries sum to $1$:

The entries in $\textbf{q}$ describe the distribution of votes at an election to be held many years from now (assuming the stochastic matrix continues to describe the changes from one election to the next). Thus, eventually, about $54\%$ of the vote will be for the Republican candidate.

note.title: Numerical Notes﻿
note.heading: Numerical Notes﻿
note.paragraph: You may have noticed that if $\textbf{x}_{k + 1} = P\textbf{x}_{k}$ for $k = 0,1,\ldots,$ then

To compute a specific vector such as $\textbf{x}_{3}$, fewer arithmetic operations are needed to compute $\textbf{x}_{1},\textbf{x}_{2}$, and $\textbf{x}_{3}$, rather than $P^{3}$ and $P^{3}\textbf{x}_{0}$. However, if $P$ is small—say, $30 \times 30$—the machine computation time is insignificant for both methods, and a command to compute $P^{3}\textbf{x}_{0}$ might be preferred because it requires fewer human keystrokes.

Of the listeners who are tuned to the news station, $70\%$ will remain listening to the news after the station break that occurs each half hour, while $30\%~$will switch to the music station at the station break. Of the listeners who are tuned to the music station, $60\%$ will switch to the news station at the station break, while $40\%$ will remain listening to the music. Suppose everyone is listening to the news at 8:15 A.M.

statement.paragraph: A laboratory animal may eat any one of three foods each day. Laboratory records show that if the animal chooses one food on one trial, it will choose the same food on the next trial with a probability of $50\%$, and it will choose the other foods on the next trial with equal probabilities of $25\%$.

list.item: What is the stochastic matrix for this situation?
If the animal chooses food #1 on an initial trial, what is the probability that it will choose food #2 on the second trial after the initial trial?

statement.paragraph: On any given day, a student is either healthy or ill. Of the students who are healthy today, $95\%$ will be healthy tomorrow. Of the students who are ill today, $55\%$ will still be ill tomorrow.

list.item: What is the stochastic matrix for this situation?
Suppose 20% of the students are ill on Monday. What fraction or percentage of the students are likely to be ill on Tuesday? On Wednesday?
If a student is well today, what is the probability that he or she will be well two days from now?

statement.paragraph: The weather in Columbus is either good, indifferent, or bad on any given day. If the weather is good today, there is a $60\%$ chance the weather will be good tomorrow, a $30\%$ chance the weather will be indifferent, and a $10\%$ chance the weather will be bad. If the weather is indifferent today, it will be good tomorrow with probability $\text{.40}$ and indifferent with probability $\text{.30}$. Finally, if the weather is bad today, it will be good tomorrow with probability $\text{.40}$ and indifferent with probability $\text{.50}$.

list.item: What is the stochastic matrix for this situation?
